Inflammable (adjective) means easily capable of catching fire and burning. If something is inflammable, it means that it can ignite — often quickly and intensely — when exposed to a flame, spark, or enough heat.

Simple test: If you need to keep something away from fire, and that thing itself will burn dangerously, you'd call it inflammable.

Gasoline, dry wood, alcohol, paper, and many chemical solvents are inflammable materials.
The Most Important Thing to Know About This Word

Here is where most people go wrong, and where you can go very right.

"Inflammable" does NOT mean "not able to catch fire."

This is the single biggest trap this word sets. In English, the prefix "in-" very commonly means not — as in:

  • invisible = not visible
  • incomplete = not complete
  • incorrect = not correct

So almost everyone's first instinct is to assume that inflammable = not flammable. That assumption is completely wrong and, in real life, it has caused serious accidents.

The truth is: "inflammable" and "flammable" mean exactly the same thing. Both words mean can catch fire easily. The "in-" here is not a negating prefix at all — it's a different kind of prefix entirely, one that simply intensifies or leads into the root word (think of the verb "to inflame," meaning to set something on fire). So "inflammable" literally means "capable of being inflamed" — i.e., capable of catching fire.
Why This Confusion Became a Real-World Safety Problem

The confusion was so widespread and so dangerous that safety authorities, particularly in industries dealing with chemicals, fuels, and hazardous goods, actually officially moved away from using "inflammable" on warning labels and replaced it with "flammable." The reason was simple: a worker, truck driver, or first responder who misread "inflammable" as meaning fire-safe could handle a dangerous substance carelessly — and pay for that mistake with their life.

So today, on petrol tankers, chemical drums, and hazmat labels, you are far more likely to see "FLAMMABLE" rather than "inflammable," specifically because "flammable" cannot be misread as a negative.

This is a rare case in language where a word was practically retired from certain contexts simply because it was too confusing to be safe.

Here is how "inflammable" is naturally used:

  • The warehouse was filled with inflammable liquids, so smoking was strictly prohibited.
  • Dry grass in summer becomes highly inflammable.
  • The label warned that the cleaning product was inflammable and should be stored away from heat sources.
  • Firefighters are trained to identify inflammable materials at the scene of an emergency.

Notice that "highly inflammable" is a common and perfectly correct phrase — something that catches fire very easily.

If inflammable means can catch fire, the opposite is:

  • Non-flammable — cannot catch fire under normal conditions
  • Fire-resistant — resists catching fire, though not completely immune
  • Fireproof — will not burn at all (extremely rare in practice)
A Figurative Use (Less Common, But Real)

"Inflammable" can also be used metaphorically, beyond physical fire. When a situation is described as inflammable, it means it is dangerously unstable and could "explode" into conflict, violence, or crisis at any moment.

  • The political tensions in the region were inflammable — one wrong move could set off a catastrophe.
  • His temper was inflammable; the slightest criticism sent him into a rage.

This figurative use is less frequent, but you will encounter it in literature and journalism.

• Inflammably (adverb): in a manner that can catch fire. "The material burned inflammably fast."
  • Inflammability (noun): the quality or degree to which something can catch fire. "The inflammability of the building's insulation was a serious concern."
The One-Line Summary to Lock It In
Inflammable = flammable = catches fire easily. The "in-" does NOT mean "not." When in doubt, treat anything labeled "inflammable" as dangerously combustible — because it is.
